name: Mastic / hard gum

lead: Mastic gum is a hard, chewy resin from the mastic tree (Pistacia lentiscus) grown mainly on the Greek island of Chios, and it is marketed alongside harder-than-normal gums such as Turkish falim as a jaw-training gum. Several brands now sell mastic-based jawline gum.
It is used in looksmaxxing circles as a food-based way to work the masseter and encourage a more defined lower face.

paras: Prolonged hard chewing makes the masseter and temporalis work against resistance, which may raise muscle stiffness, endurance and possibly size over time. The resin itself has traditional digestive uses, but any jaw effect is attributed to the chewing load, not the substance.

No controlled study shows mastic gum sculpts the jawline; small studies cover muscle stiffness and oxygen dynamics, not definition. Heavy chewing is associated with jaw muscle pain, TMJ strain and uneven wear, and larger masseters broaden rather than sharpen the face. Forum users themselves raise TMJ concerns, and the jawline effect is unproven.

web.title: Masticatory muscle stiffness after gum chewing (PMC)

lead: Mastic gum is a chewable resin obtained from the mastic tree (Pistacia lentiscus var. chia), cultivated mainly on the southern part of the Greek island of Chios, and it is also the base of several commercial chewing gums.[1] In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed, together with other firm or long-lasting gums such as Turkish-style hard gum and branded 'jawline' gums, as a way to give the jaw muscles resistance training in the hope of a more defined lower face.[2][3][4]

The resin itself has a long history in Mediterranean traditional medicine, particularly for digestive complaints, and has been examined in small clinical trials for stomach and duodenal conditions.[1][5][6][7] Those studies concern digestive and other health outcomes, not facial appearance.

No published controlled study has tested whether chewing mastic or other hard gum changes jaw shape or facial definition in healthy adults. Related research is limited to short-term measurements of masseter muscle stiffness and oxygen dynamics after chewing, and to epidemiological work on gum chewing and temporomandibular disorder.[8][9][10]
infobox: Pistacia lentiscus var. chia resin (Chios, Greece)
Described by Grokipedia as a traditional herbal medicinal product for mild dyspepsia in the EU (2015)[1]

paras: Mastic is an aromatic resin that hardens into small pale tears after being exuded from incisions in the bark of the mastic tree.[1] Chios mastic has held an EU protected designation of origin since 1997 and its traditional harvesting method was added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2014, according to one encyclopedic summary.[1] The resin is chewed as a gum, used in liqueurs, confectionery and baking, and in cosmetics and perfumery.[1]

Chemical analyses identify a volatile fraction rich in alpha-pinene, myrcene and beta-caryophyllene, and a resin fraction made largely of triterpenoids.[1][11][12] Commercial 'jawline' gums sold to the looksmaxxing market typically use a mastic or other dense gum base marketed as harder to chew than supermarket gum; one such product was the subject of a looksmax.org thread asking whether users had tried it.[4]

In forum discussion, hard gum is presented as a food-based alternative to dedicated jaw exercisers. The idea is that sustained, forceful chewing loads the masseter and temporalis muscles, which proponents hope will thicken the muscle and sharpen the jaw or lower face. Threads on looksmax.org compare mastic with regular gum and gather chewing advice in a long-running megathread.[2][3]
Brand-name gums marketed for the jaw have appeared in forum threads in which users ask about others' experiences.[4]

No randomized or controlled trial has examined mastic or hard gum for jawline definition, masseter size or facial contour in healthy adults. The nearest evidence concerns acute muscle responses. A study of 40 healthy adults measured masseter and temporalis stiffness with shear wave elastography before, immediately after, and ten minutes after chewing gum for ten minutes; masseter stiffness rose after chewing and fell again after rest, and the authors noted the study was small, short-term and included only healthy volunteers.[8] A separate 2024 report examined the effect of gum chewing training on masseter muscle oxygen dynamics.[9] Neither study measured facial shape.

Chewing gum increases masticatory muscle activity, and researchers distinguish this from muscle hypertrophy or changes in bone contour; the published work above does not address whether the former leads to the latter.

A 2014 study examined the association between temporomandibular disorder (TMD) and gum chewing.[10] Jaw clinicians commonly list habitual or prolonged chewing among behaviours to review in people with jaw-joint or muscle pain, and users on looksmax.org have themselves raised temporomandibular joint concerns in chewing discussions.[10][3]

Mastic is an Anacardiaceae resin, and a study of 288 sera screened for IgG and IgE antibodies to a panel of gums, including mastic gum, noting that gums have a history of sensitivity reactions.[13] Hard or sticky gum may also affect dental restorations. Larger masseters would be expected to broaden rather than narrow the lower face, a point raised in forum discussion of jaw training generally.[3]

sections.h: Medical and traditional uses of mastic
paras: Outside appearance, mastic gum has been studied for digestive complaints. A 1984 double-blind trial compared mastic with placebo in duodenal ulcer, and a 2010 randomized, double-blind trial tested Chios mastic gum in functional dyspepsia.[5][6] A 2020 review summarizes traditional uses, phytochemistry and pharmacology,[7] and laboratory work has examined activity against Helicobacter pylori, oxidation of LDL and colon cancer cells.[14][15] A 2024 review discusses antidiabetic properties of the plant,[16] and a 2026 randomized trial (HYPER-MASTIC) evaluated Chios mastic supplementation in well-controlled hypertension.[17] These results relate to mastic as a supplement or medicine and not to the mechanical effects of chewing.[5][6][7]

No studies found on mastic or hard gum for jaw or facial appearance. Related human research is limited to a ten-minute chewing study of masseter stiffness in 40 healthy adults,[8] a report on masseter oxygen dynamics after gum-chewing training,[9] and an epidemiological study of gum chewing and TMD.[10] Separate randomized trials of mastic for dyspepsia, duodenal ulcer and hypertension concern non-cosmetic outcomes.[5][6][17]
